s-fc6-high-0.essay:
In Kazuo Ishiguro's The Remains of the Day, Stevens, an aging English butler, believes that a great butler never lets his private self show. He calls this ideal "dignity," and for most of the novel his silence looks like professional discipline. What Stevens refuses to say, though, is exactly what he cannot afford to know: that he loved Miss Kenton, and that the master he served so loyally was wrong. His silence protects the story of a life well spent, but because the whole novel is narrated by Stevens himself, the silence keeps exposing him to the reader. Ishiguro uses that gap to argue that a life built on restraint can empty out the very loyalty it claims to honor.

The clearest early example is the night of the 1923 conference at Darlington Hall, when Stevens's father is dying upstairs. Stevens keeps serving the guests and won't go up, and when he describes the evening years later he calls it a kind of triumph. Some guests notice he looks upset, and he blames it on the strain of the work. Here the silence is double. He withholds grief from the people around him, and in the narration he holds it back from himself by turning the memory into a story about professional achievement. The reader can see what Stevens won't name. A son couldn't leave the dining room to say goodbye to his father, and that is not dignity but loss.

The same pattern shapes his relationship with Miss Kenton, and here Ishiguro builds the silence into the structure of the scenes. When she finds him reading a sentimental romance and tries to see what it is, Stevens refuses to show her, and he later explains to us that he only reads such books to improve his English. The explanation tells on him. A man who has nothing to hide does not need an excuse that careful. The worst moment comes after Miss Kenton tells him she has accepted Mr. Benn's proposal. Stevens stands outside her door, sure that she is crying, and he does not knock. He walks away and goes back to his duties. Ishiguro gives us the door as a physical image of everything Stevens won't say, a barrier he could open and chooses not to.

What makes the novel more than a sad love story is that Stevens's personal silences match his political ones. When Lord Darlington orders him to dismiss two Jewish maids, Stevens does it without objecting, though he later claims he was privately against it. On his trip in 1956, he even denies to strangers that he ever worked for Lord Darlington. One might read this denial as simple shame, but it works more like the closed door. To admit the connection would mean admitting that his loyalty helped a man who sympathized with the Nazis, and that would ruin the meaning of his whole career. In this way Ishiguro connects one butler's habit of keeping quiet to a larger English culture of deference, where obedience can let wrong things happen without anyone ever approving them out loud.

The novel finally lets the silence crack, but only for a moment. When Stevens meets Miss Kenton, now Mrs. Benn, at the end of his trip, she admits she has sometimes imagined the life she might have had with him. Stevens tells the reader that his heart was breaking, and then says nothing of the sort to her. Later, on the pier at Weymouth, he cries in front of a stranger, and then talks himself into practicing bantering for his new American employer, Mr. Farraday. That ending is painfully ambiguous. It could be a small step toward human connection, or it could be one more way to fill a silence without saying anything. Either way, Ishiguro shows that the restraint Stevens took for dignity has cost him the father, the woman, and the moral judgment it was supposed to protect, and that the only person who hears all of it is the reader.

s-fc6-high-1.essay:
Stevens, the butler who narrates Kazuo Ishiguro's The Remains of the Day, believes that silence is what a great butler is made of. He calls it "dignity," the ability never to step out of his professional role in front of others. But the novel shows that his refusals to speak protect him from more than embarrassment. Stevens's silences about his father, about Miss Kenton, and about Lord Darlington are the way he hides from the fact that he has given his whole life to a man and a role that did not deserve it. Ishiguro builds the novel so that the reader hears what Stevens leaves out. In the end his silence tells the reader the truth he spends the whole road trip avoiding, even though it was supposed to hide it.

The first major silence comes when Stevens's father has a stroke during the important international conference at Darlington Hall in 1923. Stevens does not go to his father's bedside. He keeps serving port to the guests, and when a guest notices he looks upset, he gives a polite non-answer and keeps working. Even in the narration he barely describes his feelings. He moves quickly to telling us that he looks back on the night with a sense of triumph. The gap between what happened and the word he picks for it is the point. Stevens can't admit he is grieving, so the narration skips over it, but the details he does include, like the guest asking if he is unwell, give him away. The professional silence that is supposed to make him dignified actually leaves the reader seeing a son who missed his father's death and is calling that an achievement.

His silence with Miss Kenton works the same way but costs more because it goes on for years. When she tells him she has accepted a proposal of marriage, he responds with formal congratulations and goes back to his duties. Later he passes her door and believes she is crying inside, and he stands there without knocking. Ishiguro gives us that moment through Stevens's own memory, and Stevens even seems unsure about which evening it happened on. That uncertainty matters. It suggests he has gone over the memory so many times, and blurred it, because looking at it clearly would mean admitting he loved her. Years later, when they meet near the end of the novel, she admits she has sometimes imagined the life she might have had with him. Stevens tells the reader that at that moment his heart was breaking, but he does not say it to her. The reader is the only one who hears it, which makes his silence feel both protective and tragic. He is loyal to his idea of dignity and also too afraid to speak, and the novel won't let us call it only one of those.

The darkest silence is about Lord Darlington himself. When Darlington orders two Jewish maids dismissed, Stevens carries out the order without objecting, while Miss Kenton protests. Later Stevens says he was troubled by it too, and she asks him why he never said so. On his trip, he even tells Mrs. Wakefield, and allows others he meets to believe, that he did not work for Darlington. Stevens says he denies it to avoid hearing gossip, but the reader can see a deeper reason. Darlington had sympathized with the Nazis and was disgraced, and if Stevens admitted that, he would be admitting that his "dignity" served something shameful. Some readers might defend Stevens as a product of a class system that trained servants not to have opinions, and the novel does show that pressure. But Ishiguro also has Miss Kenton speak up from the same position, so Stevens cannot be fully excused.

By the end, sitting on the pier, Stevens briefly cries in front of a stranger and admits he trusted Darlington's wisdom. It is the closest he comes to speaking. Then he decides to practice bantering for his new employer, and so he goes back to performing his role. Ishiguro suggests that a life built on silence can't easily be undone, and the remains of Stevens's day are spent keeping it up.

s-fc6-mid-0.work_chosen: The Great Gatsby, F. Scott Fitzgerald
s-fc6-mid-0.essay:
In The Great Gatsby, Jay Gatsby is a man who talks constantly about his past in the form of stories, but what he never says is just as important. His silence about where he really came from and about what he wants from Daisy shows that he cannot admit his whole identity is built on a dream he knows is slipping away. Through Gatsby's silences, Fitzgerald suggests that the American Dream is something people protect by refusing to look at it directly, and that this refusal is what finally destroys them.

One of the clearest examples is how Gatsby avoids the truth about his background. Nick learns that he was born James Gatz of North Dakota, but Gatsby tells people he is an Oxford man from a wealthy family in the Midwest. When Nick or others ask how he made his money, he gives vague answers or just changes the subject, and he never explains his connection to Meyer Wolfsheim. This silence protects him from being seen as new money and a criminal, but it also shows that he cannot accept who he was. He has to keep the invented Gatsby alive in order to deserve Daisy, so the silence is really about shame. Fitzgerald uses Nick as narrator to let the reader notice these gaps, since Nick reports the stories and then hints that he does not fully believe them.

The silence is also about Daisy. Gatsby never openly says that he is trying to repeat the past, and he asks Nick to arrange the tea so that he does not have to just ask her himself. Later, he wants Daisy to say she never loved Tom, which is a kind of demand that cannot be said out loud as a plain request. When Daisy cannot say it, Gatsby does not respond by facing the truth. He goes quiet and keeps believing, telling Nick that of course she will come back. Here the silence keeps alive a story he needs to believe, just as the prompt describes. The green light across the water works the same way as a symbol, because it stands for something he never fully speaks about but which controls everything he does.

In the end, Gatsby's silence also takes a toll on him. Because he never says what he really wants, or what he really is, no one around him knows him, and few people come to his funeral. Even Daisy stays silent after the accident, and she lets Gatsby take the blame, so her silence is a more selfish one than his. The comparison shows that silence can be loyalty in one person and cowardice in another.

Overall, the silences in the novel reveal that Gatsby's dream is partly a lie he tells himself. What he leaves unsaid isolates him and makes his hope impossible to correct, which is why the novel reads as both a tragedy and a criticism of the dream itself.

annotations.quote: His silence about where he really came from and about what he wants from Daisy shows that he cannot admit his whole identity is built on a dream he knows is slipping away.
annotations.comment: Defensible thesis that names what the silence hides and links it to a reading of the whole novel (the American Dream). Earns the thesis point, though 'knows is slipping away' is a bit overstated.

annotations.quote: he gives vague answers or just changes the subject, and he never explains his connection to Meyer Wolfsheim
annotations.comment: Specific, accurate moments of evasion, and the commentary ties them to shame and to Gatsby's invented identity. However, the examples are brief and not tied to particular scenes, so the evidence is only partly specific.

annotations.quote: Fitzgerald uses Nick as narrator to let the reader notice these gaps
annotations.comment: Gestures at narrative technique (Nick's perspective) as a way of conveying the silence, but the point is thin and not developed with an example.

annotations.quote: The green light across the water works the same way as a symbol
annotations.comment: Names a symbol but explains it only generally; the link to withheld speech is asserted rather than analyzed, so technique is discussed thinly.

annotations.quote: Even Daisy stays silent after the accident, and she lets Gatsby take the blame, so her silence is a more selfish one than his.
annotations.comment: Contrast between Gatsby's silence and Daisy's shows some awareness of complexity (loyalty vs. cowardice), but it is a single paragraph-ending observation and is not sustained through the essay, so it falls short of sophistication.

annotations.quote: Gatsby's dream is partly a lie he tells himself
annotations.comment: The conclusion restates the thesis in general terms; the interpretation is reasonable but repetitive and does not add new insight or consider alternative readings.

s-fc6-mid-1.essay:
In The Remains of the Day, Stevens the butler almost never says what he feels, and the things he avoids saying show what he cannot admit: that his devotion to "dignity" and to Lord Darlington cost him love and any real life of his own. Ishiguro makes Stevens's silence protect him, but it also traps him, and this shapes the whole novel into a story about wasted years that the narrator only half understands.

The clearest example is Stevens's relationship with Miss Kenton. Throughout their years at Darlington Hall she tries to get him to react, and he keeps answering with talk about work. When she finds him reading a book in his pantry, he reacts as if she has invaded his privacy instead of telling her why it matters to him. Later, when she tells him she has been offered a proposal of marriage, Stevens only says it is none of his business and congratulates her. She is clearly hoping he will say something else. His silence here is polite, but it is also a refusal, and Miss Kenton leaves as a result. Ishiguro lets the reader see how much Stevens feels, because the novel is told in first person and Stevens himself keeps changing the subject back to professional matters. The gap between what he narrates and what the reader understands is the main technique that makes the silence meaningful.

His silence about his father works the same way. During the important conference at Darlington Hall, Stevens's father is dying upstairs, and Stevens keeps doing his duties. He tells Miss Kenton that he cannot leave his post, and he does not cry or speak of grief. Stevens later describes the night as a kind of "triumph," which shows that he has turned a painful loss into proof of his professionalism. The silence lets him believe a story he needs, which is that his sacrifice was worth it.

Stevens's silence about Lord Darlington is the most complicated. He never openly admits that Darlington's sympathy for the Germans was wrong, and he even denies having worked for him when strangers ask on his trip. This is loyalty, but it is also cowardice, since he does not want to face that his life's service went to a mistaken man. When he finally tells a stranger on the pier that he gave what he had to Lord Darlington, and says "I can't even say I made my own mistakes," it is the closest he comes to saying it aloud.

In the end the silence is not only a flaw in Stevens, it is the whole meaning of the book. By withholding speech, Stevens kept himself safe from pain but also from happiness, and the reader is the only one who hears everything he leaves out. The ending, where he decides to practice bantering, suggests he may be learning to speak, but it is unclear if it is too late.
